results.summary: This design is a clock divider that uses a counter and a ROM to generate one of 27 output frequencies from a 50 MHz input. The ROM stores division parameters selected by a 4-bit input, and it outputs a 28-bit value to configure the counter. To use it, a 50 MHz oscillator is needed, and the output can be observed with an oscilloscope or fed into a microcontroller. The design is a simple frequency synthesizer based on a look-up table.

Tiny Zuse is a minimal floating-point unit inspired by the Zuse Z3, supporting addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and square root. It communicates over a 9600 baud UART, where commands are sent as bytes to load registers and perform operations; results are read back in a 3-byte format. The design was tested with basic addition and a subset of the provided testbench, and silicon tests confirmed correct operation. It requires only the on-board UART connection to a host for control.

This project implements a digital three-phase generator that produces three square-wave outputs with 120-degree phase shifts from a single input clock. It uses a 3-bit Johnson counter and provides both normal and complementary outputs. The design was simulated in Quartus II and tested on an Altera Cyclone II FPGA, but it requires external signal generation and an oscilloscope for verification. The intended application is to drive three-phase motors after analog filtering, although the chip only outputs digital signals.

This is a two-player countdown timer game where players must guess when a hidden timer reaches a target time. The game uses four buttons for start, reset, and player inputs, and displays the timer on a 7-segment display. After both players have pressed their buttons, the displayed times are shown. It requires an external PMOD 7-segment display and a PMOD button module for operation.

This is an 8-bit single-cycle CPU based on Ramyad Hadidi's 'CPU In a Week' design, extended with CLR and MUL instructions. It includes a register file and an ALU, and supports basic ALU operations, load/store, and status checks, but lacks a program counter and external memory. The processor is tested through 12 testbenches covering basic functionality, though timing interactions are not fully verified. It is purely a simulation model with no external hardware interface.

This design performs grayscale conversion and Sobel edge detection on an image. It receives pixel data via an SPI interface and can be configured for bypass, grayscale, Sobel, or combined processing. An internal LFSR can generate test pixels. The output is a single processed pixel per input, and external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi is needed to send data over SPI.

This is an analog distortion pedal circuit consisting of eight opamps in series, each of which can be bypassed via digital inputs to control the amount of distortion. It operates from a 1.8V supply and produces distortion by overdriving the opamps. External hardware including capacitors, resistors, and jacks is required for input biasing and output connection. Silicon testing showed partial functionality, with distortion observed only up to the first two amplifiers.

This project implements an FIR filter with adaptable coefficients that can be configured via a serial interface. The filter uses a symmetric step response to reduce memory requirements, and coefficients can be updated by enabling a configuration mode. It has been tested with impulse and step responses, and requires an external microcontroller or simple buttons for configuration and data input. The design is useful for learning about digital filters.

This is a simple implementation of the Snake game with VGA output. The snake can be controlled with four buttons, and the game resets upon collision. It requires a 25.179 MHz clock for correct VGA timing and uses a Tiny VGA PMOD for output. Silicon testing confirmed that it works correctly.

This is a synthesized time-to-digital converter (TDC) that measures the time delay between a start signal and the clock using an interleaved delay line. The captured result is muxed out byte by byte via output pins. It requires two external signal generators to provide the start signal and clock with a known delay. Silicon testing showed partial functionality, with bits changing when a ~7ns delay was applied.
